note: THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST is 'fltTable2 gets its missing 2^-8 back'. The object's table has no 2^-8 and holds 2^-9 twice, so a generated table differs only for a magnitude that reaches entry ten -- which is why 0.00390625f is in `fbEdge` by name rather than by luck. SECOND is the pair of truncation rows: bits[19] and bits[30] carry a whole dword narrowed to a short, and with the 0/1 values a flag fixture would use, `(short)x` and `x != 0` are the same function (7458). WHAT NO ROW HERE REACHES: a NaN or an infinity in any of the five floats, whose ordered `fcom` comparisons read unordered as `below` under -mno-ieee-fp and would need a gccdiverge entry; a `word_10c` above six, which is the other caller's problem (D570/D790); and a bit buffer shorter than the message, which is out of bounds on both sides.

why: MEASURED AND WRONG, AND KEPT FOR THAT REASON.  The object shifts the rate with `sar`, so the variable is signed and `getDataBitRate` returns `int` -- but only FIVE bits are extracted, and bits 0..4 of a 32-bit value are the same under an arithmetic and a logical right shift whatever its sign.  A negative rate is driven (block value 4, long arm, rate -16) and cannot separate the two.  The same argument covers the four-bit group numbers and the thirteen-bit short_14; the `sar` is a codegen-tier reading throughout, not a behavioural one.

label: the row dump prints sixteen of the seventeen

why: The mask word is loaded with `movzwl` in the object and shifted with `sar`, which is what the cast spells; but only bits 0..15 are ever extracted, so the sign extension cannot reach an output. The reading is a codegen-tier one (CLAUDE.md's 613 rule) and no differential trial can separate the two. It is here so that a later reader can see it was measured and found unobservable rather than never asked.
label: the mask word is sign-extended rather than zero-extended

why: `short_14` is thirteen bits wide in the message and sixteen in the field, and bits 0..12 of a 16-bit value are the same whether it is sign- or zero-extended into an int. The object's `movswl` is faithful to the field's declared type and is written that way; no input can separate the two readings.
